title: Breakfast Here, Bedtime There
summary_zh: 一次跨国视频通话，为什么两边的钟不同？
story:
Maya wants to call her cousin, who lives far away. She chooses a time after dinner and sends a message: Can we talk now?

Her cousin replies later. Sorry. I was asleep.

Pip checks Maya's clock. It was not bedtime here. Perhaps the cousin's clock needs new batteries.

Leo brings out the globe from their day-and-night lesson. Different parts of Earth face the Sun at different times, he reminds them.

Ms. Park explains that people use time zones to organize local clock time. When it is evening in one place, another place may be in the morning or even on a different calendar date.

The club opens a world-clock display and chooses the actual cities. They do not guess the time difference from memory.

Some places also change their clocks during part of the year, Ms. Park says. Checking the date matters.

Maya writes two times on the invitation, one for each city, and includes the date. This time, her cousin joins while eating breakfast.

I am having toast, the cousin says.

I have already had dinner, Maya replies.

Pip holds up an empty plate. I am available for any meal in any time zone.

They laugh and compare the light outside their windows.

After the call, Leo writes a planning rule: A good meeting time is a good time for everyone, not just the person sending the invitation.
fact: Time zones help people coordinate local clock times around the rotating Earth. Their boundaries follow human decisions as well as geography. Some places use seasonal clock changes and others do not. For a real call, checking both cities and the date is more reliable than assuming a fixed difference.
recap: Maya's first invitation ignored her cousin's local time. The club checked a world clock and wrote both local times and the date. Breakfast and after-dinner conversation could then happen in the same call.
phrases: What time is it where you are?
Does this time work for you?
Let us check the date, too.
question: Why did Maya include two local times on the second invitation?
answer: The callers lived in different time zones, so each needed to know when to join using their own local clock.
wonder: What would you show a faraway friend during a short video tour of your neighborhood?

title: Chocolate Before the Candy Bar
summary_zh: 巧克力不是从糖果包装里长出来的，它的旅程从可可树开始。

words.pod: 荚状果实；此处指可可果

story:
Leo brings a chocolate wrapper to the club's Food Journeys project. He draws an arrow from a store to his mouth.

Finished, he says.

Maya adds an empty space before the store. Where did the ingredients come from?

They visit a botanical garden exhibit about cacao. A photograph shows large pods growing on a tree. Inside the pods are seeds surrounded by pale pulp.

Those seeds are the beginning of chocolate's journey, the guide explains.

Pip looks at the picture. The tree forgot the shiny wrappers.

The guide describes several steps used in making chocolate. Seeds are fermented and dried. They are often roasted, and the inner parts are ground. Different recipes add ingredients such as sugar or milk.

Leo smells a sample of unsweetened cocoa. It smells familiar, but the guide explains that cacao material is naturally bitter. Sweet candy bars get much of their sweetness from added sugar.

So chocolate flavor and sweetness are different things, Maya says.

They learn that cacao has a long history in the Americas, including use in drinks before modern candy bars existed.

Leo expands his drawing into a chain of people and places: growers, processors, makers, transport, and stores.

Pip adds one final box: curious eater.

That is me, says Leo.

Maya smiles. Now your arrow has a story behind it.

Leo agrees, although he still likes the final part of the journey best.
fact: Chocolate begins with seeds from cacao pods. Processing develops its familiar flavor, and recipes determine how much sugar, milk, or other ingredients are added. Cacao has a long history in the Americas. A sweet chocolate bar is a finished product with a much longer story behind it.
recap: The chocolate journey began with a tree rather than a store. The club followed seeds through several processing steps and distinguished cacao's flavor from added sweetness. Leo's simple arrow became a chain of people and processes.
phrases: Where does it come from?
What happens before this step?
Many people help make it.
question: Which part of the cacao plant is used to begin making chocolate?
answer: The seeds inside cacao pods are used.
wonder: Choose one food you ate today. How far back can you trace its ingredients?

title: The Triangle Team
summary_zh: 桥梁和屋架为什么常出现三角形？
story:
The club builds shapes with strips of cardboard joined at the corners. Leo makes a square. Maya makes a triangle.

Pip declares the square the winner because it has more corners.

Ms. Park asks them to push gently on the shapes. The square changes into a slanted shape as its corner joints turn. Maya's triangle keeps its shape more easily without bending the strips.

The number of corners was not a useful test, Pip admits.

Maya adds a diagonal strip across the square. Now it is divided into two triangles, and it resists the same gentle push better.

They look at pictures of bridge frameworks and roof supports. Triangles appear again and again.

Does that mean every bridge must be a triangle? Leo asks.

No, says Ms. Park. Engineers use many kinds of structures. The material, connections, shape, and expected loads all matter.

The club improves a cardboard tower for its exhibition. They add braces where the frame was leaning and test it with the same small load as before.

Pip designs a banner: Team Triangle. Excellent at standing still.

Leo asks whether he should make his sandwich triangular for extra strength.

That depends on your engineering goal, Maya replies.

My goal is to eat it.

Then cutting it into triangles may help your lunch, she says, but it will not prove anything about bridge safety.

Pip records another important design lesson: Always ask what problem you are trying to solve.
fact: A triangle made of fixed-length sides is geometrically rigid, while a four-sided frame with freely turning corners can change shape. A diagonal brace can divide such a frame into triangles. Real structural strength also depends on materials, connections, and loads; shape alone is not a complete safety test.
recap: The square frame shifted at its joints. A diagonal brace made it resist that movement better. The children connected the model with real structures while remembering that engineering involves more than a single shape.
phrases: What problem are we trying to solve?
This brace helps support the frame.
Let us test it with the same load.
question: What did Maya add to help the square frame keep its shape?
answer: She added a diagonal brace, dividing the square into two triangles.
wonder: Where can you find triangles used as part of a structure around you?

title: A Message Made of Flashes
summary_zh: 灯光怎样变成消息？先让双方理解同一套规则。
story:
The classroom is divided into two pretend islands. Maya stands on one side with a small flashlight. Leo stands on the other with a notebook.

No shouting across the ocean, Ms. Park says. Your challenge is to send a message with light.

Maya flashes three times. Leo writes: Three snacks, please.

That is not what I meant, she says.

Pip writes: Three robots arriving.

Also wrong.

They realize they need an agreed code. They choose one short flash for yes and two short flashes for no. A longer pause separates messages.

Now Ms. Park asks questions. Is the library open? One flash. Is Pip a penguin? Two flashes.

Pip requests a third answer: Occasionally, during dance practice.

The children later try a simple letter chart. They discover that sending letters takes patience and that unclear pauses can change the message.

Ms. Park explains that people have used many kinds of signals to carry information, including light, sound, and electrical pulses. A code connects patterns with meanings.

Leo deliberately sends one unclear pattern. Maya asks him to repeat it instead of guessing.

That is good communication, Ms. Park says. Checking a message can be part of the system.

Pip sends two careful flashes and then holds up a sign: No penguins detected.

Leo looks relieved. The classroom ocean is safe for another day.
fact: A signal can carry information when sender and receiver share a rule for interpreting it. Codes assign meanings to patterns. Timing and separation can matter as much as the individual signals. Real communication systems also need ways to handle errors or ask for information to be sent again.
recap: Random flashes produced different guesses. Once the children agreed on a code and pauses, they could exchange messages. When a pattern was unclear, asking for a repeat worked better than inventing an answer.
phrases: What does this signal mean?
Could you send that again?
We need the same set of rules.
question: Why did the first three flashes fail to communicate Maya's meaning?
answer: The group had not agreed on a code, so each person gave the flashes a different meaning.
wonder: What simple signal could your family use to mean that someone needs a quiet moment?

title: The Bicycle with the Giant Wheel
summary_zh: 旧式高轮自行车很引人注目，但好设计还要考虑使用者。
story:
At a transport museum, Leo stops beside a bicycle with an enormous front wheel and a tiny back wheel.

The wheels forgot to agree on a size, he says.

Pip studies the high seat. I would need a ladder and a very encouraging friend.

The museum educator explains that on many high-wheel bicycles, the pedals directly turned the large front wheel. A larger wheel traveled farther with each turn, but the high riding position brought difficulties and risks.

Maya compares it with a later bicycle in the next display. That one has two more similar-sized wheels and a chain drive.

The chain carries motion from the pedals to the rear wheel, the educator says. This arrangement helped designers use a lower riding position.

So the old bicycle was not simply silly, Maya says. It was part of people trying different solutions.

Exactly. An invention has a history of ideas, trade-offs, and improvements.

The club sketches an imaginary future bicycle. Leo adds a rain cover. Maya adds a place for a schoolbag that will not interfere with riding. Pip adds automatic applause whenever the rider climbs a hill.

How heavy would all that make it? the educator asks.

They pause. Every extra feature has a cost.

Pip removes the large applause machine and replaces it with one small bell.

A lighter celebration, he says.

Maya writes their design question: Better for whom, and better at what?
fact: Many historic high-wheel bicycles connected the pedals directly to the front wheel. Later chain-driven designs helped make lower bicycles with more similar wheel sizes practical. Design changes involve trade-offs among speed, comfort, control, weight, and other goals. Newer does not explain which particular feature solves a problem.
recap: The giant wheel reflected an earlier design approach. Comparing it with a chain-driven bicycle showed how mechanisms and riding position changed. The club then discovered that adding features to its own design also added trade-offs.
phrases: How did this design work?
What problem did the change solve?
It is useful, but it adds weight.
question: Why did the club remove its large applause machine from the bicycle design?
answer: It added too much weight for a small benefit, so they chose a lighter feature.
wonder: What one improvement would make an everyday object easier for you to use?

title: Pip Follows the Wrong Instructions
summary_zh: 机器人严格照做，却没有到达目的地，问题出在哪里？
story:
Maya draws a grid on a large sheet of paper. A star marks the destination. Pip will follow a short program to reach it.

Leo writes: Move forward two squares. Turn right. Move forward one square.

Pip follows the instructions and arrives beside a picture of a banana.

That is not the star, Maya says.

Pip checks his record. I followed every instruction.

They examine the starting position. Leo imagined Pip facing the top of the page, but Pip was facing left.

We forgot to specify the starting direction, Maya realizes.

They add it and run the same sequence again. This time, Pip reaches the star.

Next, Leo writes a longer program. One turn is wrong, so Pip ends up at the banana again.

The banana is very popular today, says Pip.

Instead of rewriting everything at random, the children trace each step with a finger. They find the incorrect turn and change it.

That process of finding and fixing problems is called debugging, Ms. Park explains.

Maya asks whether a computer always understands what a person really intends.

It carries out the operations its system is built to perform, says Ms. Park. Clear instructions and checking results still matter.

Pip completes the route at last. He requests one final instruction: Celebrate politely.

Leo writes it more precisely: Ring your bell once.

Pip rings twice.

Everyone looks at him.

A joke, he says. Please do not debug my sense of humor.
fact: An algorithm is a sequence of steps for carrying out a task. The starting conditions can affect its result. Debugging means locating and correcting problems in a program. Tracing one step at a time helps connect what the instructions say with what actually happens.
recap: The first route failed because the starting direction was unclear. A later route failed because one turn was wrong. The children checked the steps, found each problem, and corrected it.
phrases: Which way are you facing?
Follow one step at a time.
Let us find where it went wrong.
question: Why did Pip miss the star on the first attempt?
answer: The children had not specified the starting direction, so Pip began facing a different way from the one Leo imagined.
wonder: Could you give someone precise instructions for drawing a simple shape without showing it to them?

title: The Great Paper Airplane Claim
summary_zh: 一架飞机飞得远，就能证明它的设计一定最好吗？
story:
Leo throws a paper airplane across the classroom test area. It lands beyond Maya's plane.

My design is the best in the world, he announces.

Pip begins preparing a very large trophy.

Maya asks a question. Did we throw the planes in the same way?

Leo had a running start. Maya stood still. The paper was different, and one plane had a paper clip attached.

We changed several things, she says. We cannot tell which one made the difference.

Ms. Park helps them plan a fairer comparison. They use the same kind of paper, the same starting line, and the same person to launch both designs as consistently as possible. Everyone stays behind the line while a plane is thrown into the clear area.

They measure several flights for each design. Sometimes Leo's plane travels farther. Sometimes Maya's does.

Pip lowers the trophy to a more reasonable size.

The children compare the results and notice variation. One spectacular flight does not represent every attempt.

Leo changes his statement. In our small test, this design usually traveled farther under these conditions.

That is less dramatic, he says.

But it tells people what you actually tested, Maya replies.

Pip presents an award anyway: Best Improved Claim.

Leo accepts it. Next time, he says, I want to test which plane stays in the air longest.

Maya smiles. A different question may need a different measurement.
fact: A fair comparison tries to keep other important conditions similar while changing the feature being studied. Repeated trials reveal variation. A claim should match the evidence and the conditions of the test. Measuring distance answers a different question from measuring time in the air.
recap: Leo's first claim was much larger than his evidence. The club controlled more conditions, repeated the flights, and used careful wording. They also noticed that the meaning of best depends on what they measure.
phrases: Did we keep the conditions the same?
Let us try it more than once.
What does the evidence support?
question: Why was one long flight not enough to prove that Leo's design was the best in the world?
answer: Other conditions differed, results can vary, and the small test could not compare every design or every meaning of best.
wonder: What everyday claim would you enjoy testing with a simple, fair comparison?

title: The Museum of Better Questions
focus: 复现代词、问句与因果表达；系列回顾
summary_zh: 好奇心俱乐部办展览，把一路发现变成新的问题。
story:
The Curiosity Club opens a small exhibition for families. Maya stands beside the paper bridge. Leo manages the model boat. Pip welcomes visitors with a sign: Questions are free. Please take more than one.

A younger child points at the bridge. Is this yours?

It is ours, Maya says. We tested different folds together.

Another visitor asks why the clay boat floats. Leo explains the shape and the water it pushes aside. When he forgets a word, he uses a simple sentence and points to the model.

At the animal table, visitors guess which creature has three hearts. At the space table, a lamp and a ball show changing views of the Moon's bright side.

Pip has made a wall of earlier guesses. The Sun goes to bed. Camels keep drinking water in their humps. Penguins are fish in jackets.

Why display mistakes? a parent asks.

Because we learned to change our ideas when we found better evidence, Maya says.

The final table has blank cards. Visitors write something they would like to understand. Soon, the box is full of questions about music, oceans, buildings, and everyday life.

Leo reads one: Why do we keep asking questions?

Pip thinks carefully. Because each answer opens another door.

Maya switches off the exhibition lamp at closing time. The real Sun has not gone to bed, she reminds Leo.

I know, he says. But I am ready for dinner.

Some questions, Pip announces, return every single day.
fact: Learning can connect observation, explanation, and checking. A model helps communicate an idea, while evidence helps decide whether the explanation fits. Revising a mistaken idea is part of learning. A useful question can be small and ordinary; it does not have to be about a distant planet.
recap: The exhibition brought together bridges, boats, animals, and space. The club explained its discoveries, remembered earlier mistakes, and collected new questions. Curiosity continued after the last display was packed away.
phrases: It is ours. We made it together.
I used to think that, but now I understand.
What would you like to find out next?
question: Why did the club display some of its earlier mistaken ideas?
answer: The mistakes showed how the children changed their thinking after gathering evidence and learning more.
wonder: Which idea from the Curiosity Club would you most like to explain to someone else?
